opus-5.5.text:
Well, the basic reason is that the world is not entirely predictable, and pixels are a terrible place to try to predict it.

If you train a system to predict what happens next in a video at the pixel level, you're asking it to predict an enormous amount of detail that is essentially unpredictable: the exact texture of the carpet, how every leaf on a tree is moving in the wind, the precise ripples on a pond. There's no way to predict that, and the system will spend a huge amount of its capacity trying. We tried this for years, at FAIR and elsewhere, and what you get with a straightforward predictive model is blurry predictions, because the system averages over all the possible futures. You can try to fix that with GANs, with diffusion, with various latent-variable tricks, and some of these produce very pretty videos. But producing pretty videos and learning a good representation of the world are not the same thing. The question is whether the internal representation is useful for understanding and planning, and empirically, pixel reconstruction has not been a very good way to get there.

That's why I've been pushing joint embedding architectures, what we call JEPA, Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture. Instead of predicting the pixels of y from x, you run both x and y through encoders and predict the representation of y from the representation of x. The encoder is then free to throw away the details that aren't predictable and keep the information that is: the objects, where they are, how they're moving, the abstract structure of the scene. The prediction happens in an abstract space where it's actually feasible.

There's an obvious difficulty with that. If you just train the system to make the two representations match, it can cheat and collapse: map everything to a constant, and the prediction is perfect and useless. So a lot of the work over the last several years has gone into preventing collapse. Contrastive methods were the first approach, but they don't scale well with dimension. Then came non-contrastive methods like Barlow Twins and VICReg, which explicitly maximize the information content of the representations, and distillation-style methods with an exponential moving average target encoder, which is what I-JEPA and V-JEPA use. These work really well.

The empirical evidence lines up with the theory. For images, joint embedding methods trained with self-supervised learning give better representations for downstream tasks than reconstruction-based methods like masked autoencoders, at least when you evaluate the features without heavy fine-tuning. For video, V-JEPA learns features that capture motion and physical dynamics much more efficiently than generative approaches. And with V-JEPA 2, we showed you can use such a model for planning, for zero-shot robot manipulation, because you have a predictor operating in representation space, which is exactly what you need for model predictive control.

The deeper point is this. Text works well with generative models because language is discrete and already abstract. You can predict a probability distribution over the next token from a finite vocabulary. But video is high-dimensional and continuous, and you can't represent a distribution over all possible next frames in a tractable way. So if we want machines that understand the physical world, the way a baby or a cat does, I'm convinced the path is not through generative models of pixels. It's through learning abstract representations and predicting in that space. That's what I've been saying for a while: abandon generative models, at least for this purpose, and go with joint embedding architectures.

r001.rationale: It describes constant-output collapse when matching representations, but does not identify the identity function as a trivial solution to reconstructing the image input.

r002.rationale: It explains that JEPA encodes both observations and predicts the representation of one from the other.

r003.rationale: It says joint embedding methods produce better image representations than reconstruction methods and that V-JEPA captures video motion and dynamics more efficiently than generative approaches.

fable-5.1.text:
Because the world is not predictable at the pixel level, and trying to predict it at that level is mostly a waste of capacity.

If you take an image, mask out a chunk of it, and train a network to reconstruct the missing pixels, the model has to spend most of its effort on things that are fundamentally unpredictable: the exact texture of the grass, the precise placement of every leaf, the noise in the sensor. There are infinitely many plausible completions. If you train with a squared-error loss, you get a blurry average. If you train a generative model to sample from the distribution, you end up spending enormous resources modeling details that carry almost no information about what is actually going on in the scene. The details are irrelevant to understanding, but they dominate the loss.

With video it gets much worse. Nobody can predict the exact pixels of the next second of a video. The approaches that try to do this produce things that look fine for a few frames and then fall apart, and the representations they learn are not very good for downstream tasks. People have tried this for fifteen years. It does not work as well as you would hope.

So the alternative is to do the prediction in representation space rather than in pixel space. That is the idea behind what we call joint embedding predictive architectures, JEPA. You take the input, run it through an encoder. You take the thing you want to predict, run it through another encoder. And then you train a predictor to predict the representation of the second from the representation of the first. The encoder is free to throw away the stuff that is unpredictable. It does not have to represent the exact position of every blade of grass, because the predictor cannot predict it anyway, so the system learns to abstract it out.

The difficulty, of course, is collapse. If the encoder is allowed to ignore everything, the trivial solution is to output a constant, and then prediction is perfect and useless. So the whole game in this family of methods is how you prevent collapse. You can do it with contrastive methods, pushing apart representations of different things, but those scale badly, especially in high dimension. Or you can do it with regularization that maximizes the information content of the representation, which is what things like VICReg do, or with asymmetric architectures and distillation, which is what I-JEPA and V-JEPA use. The results in practice are that you get representations that are better for tasks like classification, segmentation, depth, with far less compute than reconstruction-based methods.

There is a deeper reason I care about this, beyond image features. If you want a system that understands the world well enough to plan, you need a world model. A world model has to predict what will happen as a consequence of an action. And you want that prediction at a level of abstraction where it is actually possible, where you can say "the cup will fall off the table" without having to render the cup. Generative pixel prediction forces you to the wrong level of abstraction. Prediction in representation space lets the system find the right one by itself.

So, briefly: generative models are trying to do something that is both too hard and not useful. Predict the abstract, discard the unpredictable. That is what the brain does too. You do not consciously predict every photon hitting your retina.

r001.rationale: The response describes a constant-output collapse solution, not the identity function as a trivial solution to reconstructing the input.

r002.rationale: It explains that JEPA predicts one observation’s encoded representation from another observation’s encoded representation.

r003.rationale: It says pixel prediction produces poor downstream representations, while representation-space prediction yields better task performance with less compute.

astra-6.text:
Because predicting every pixel is a much harder problem than learning what matters in an image or a video. The world contains an enormous amount of detail that is irrelevant to understanding it, and much of that detail is inherently unpredictable.

Imagine a video of a tree blowing in the wind. You might be able to predict how the branches will move, but you cannot predict the exact position of every leaf. If you train a system to predict pixels, you force it to spend resources modeling all those possibilities. That may be useful for generating realistic videos, but it is not necessarily the best way to learn how the world works.

What I favor is predicting in representation space. You encode the observed part of the input, encode another part, and train a predictor to predict the representation of that other part. That is the idea behind a joint embedding predictive architecture, or JEPA. The representation can retain the information that is predictable and useful, while leaving out irrelevant detail.

The difficulty is preventing collapse: if the encoder produces the same representation for everything, prediction becomes trivial. So you need constraints that keep the representations informative. But you do not need to reconstruct every pixel to achieve that.

The objective is not to produce a beautiful picture. It is to learn representations that support understanding, prediction, and eventually planning.

r001.rationale: The response mentions preventing collapse, but it does not identify the identity function as a trivial solution when reconstructing an image input.

r002.rationale: It says to encode the observed input and another part, then predict the other part’s representation from the observed representation.

r003.rationale: It favors prediction in representation space, describing pixel prediction as harder and less suited to learning useful image and video representations.

sol-6.1.text:
Because predicting every pixel is both very difficult and, for learning useful representations, largely unnecessary. If I show you a video of a room and ask what happens next, there are many things you can predict: an object will fall, a person will move toward the door. But you cannot predict the exact texture of the carpet or the precise position of every leaf outside the window. Those details are not necessarily relevant to understanding the scene.

A generative model has to spend resources modeling all of that variability. And with video, the number of plausible futures is enormous. We would like the system to learn what is predictable without being forced to account for every unpredictable detail.

That is the motivation for joint-embedding predictive architectures. You encode the observed part of an image or video, encode a target part, and train a predictor to predict the target representation. The prediction takes place in representation space, where the system can retain information about objects, their interactions, and the structure of the world while ignoring irrelevant detail.

Now, you have to prevent the representations from collapsing to a constant—that is a central challenge. But if you do it properly, you can learn representations that are useful for prediction and, ultimately, planning, without first learning to generate every pixel.

r001.rationale: The response discusses representation collapse, but does not identify the identity function as a trivial solution to image reconstruction by a sufficiently large network.

r002.rationale: It says to encode the observed part and target part, then predict the target representation from the observed representation.

r003.rationale: It contrasts difficult, unnecessary pixel-level prediction with representation prediction that captures useful structure while ignoring irrelevant detail.
